Krishna's sixteen thousand ragas, a tanpura, bansurī (or harmonium / vīṇā) and tabla rendered in the browser, with speech-to-text for the prompt and lyrics and text-to-speech to recite the words. tool_layer_mhraga/mhraaga-app/ Flutter (Dart) Android app, offline synth, talks to the live API tool_layer_mhraga/mhraaga-cloud/ web/ (site) api/ (Lambda) infra/ (CloudFormation + deploy.sh) tests/ music_engine_framework_layer/mhraaga_engine/ raga grammar, 72 melakartas, 16,000 gopī ragas, tālas, composer, LLM brief How a song is made Brief - brief.py asks OpenRouter ( z-ai/glm-5.3-flash , fallback deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash ) for a JSON plan: raga, tāla, tempo, mood, language, lead instrument and lyrics. If the model fails, keyword rules still produce a song ( source: fallback ). Raga - 30 classical ragas (vādī, samvādī, pakaḍ, time), any of the 72 melakartas, or gopī 1-16000 : ascent from one melakarta, descent from another, one of three tonics (183/233/234 Hz = 732/932/936 ÷ 4), a janya cut, vādī/samvādī a fourth or fifth apart. The model has 72x72x3 = 15,552 scale-tonic pairs; ids 1-16000 give 15,947 distinct ragas (tested), not exactly 16,000. Score - compose.py follows the classical form: alap (drone, free) -> gat (tabla enters, each avartan opens with the pakaḍ on sam, vādī/samvādī held longer, meend and kan ornaments) -> tihai (closing phrase x3 landing exactly on sam). Output is a small JSON score. Sound - the browser synthesises it (Web Audio) from physical models: plucked-string tanpura and veena, breathy bansuri, reed harmonium, tabla by its modes, a room reverb, human timing and dynamics. See docs/SOUND.md . Piano-roll view, lyrics, seek, MP3/WAV export (with the AI voice). Voice - speech-to-text (mic buttons) and text-to-speech use the browser's Web Speech API (Chrome/Edge/Safari). The browser vendor's speech service processes the audio. TTS recites the words over the music; it does not pitch syllables to the raga. t: The music engine, module by module
x: The music engine, module by module Package: music_engine_framework_layer/mhraaga_engine/ . Pure Python, no web code. The Lambda imports it; the song factory and the tests use it directly. Data flows in this order: brief (what to make) -> ragas and tala (the grammar) -> compose (the score) -> physics , gan and autotune (how it feels). prompt ─► brief.py ─► {raga, tala, tempo, mood, language, lead, lyrics} │ ragas.py ◄──────┤ get_raga() tala.py ◄── TALAS ▼ compose.py ── phrases ◄── gan.py (some phrases) │ ├─ physics.humanise() rubato, weight, meend, drift (physics.py, Box2D) ├─ autotune.score() pull pitch to the shruti (autotune.py) ▼ score JSON { sa, drone, lead[], tabla[], lyrics[], sections[], meta } compose.py — the score composer compose(raga, tala="", tempo=72, duration=90, lyrics="", seed=None, sa=None, lead="bansuri", instrumental=False, poem=False, human=True) -> dict A raga is treated as a grammar, so the song follows the classical form: Section What happens alap Drone only, free time. The raga unfolds from Sa upward in stages, resting on the vadi every third phrase, with long notes (1.8 to 3 beats) and meend. About 20% of the song, at most 36 s (a poem keeps a longer alap to leave room for the spoken words). gat The tabla enters. Each avartan (tala cycle) opens on sam with the start of the pakad (at most 45% of the cycle, and 60% every third cycle, so it is stated but never fills the cycle), then alternates rise and fall phrases. The vadi and samvadi are held twice as long. The second half of the song moves faster (more half-beat notes). 30% of the time a GAN phrase replaces a rise/fall. tihai The closing figure (the end of the pakad, ending on Sa) is played three times with gaps sized so that the last note lands exactly on sam. Notes are [time, hz, duration, ornament] (then velocity and glide are added by physics). Ornament: 0 plain, 1 meend (slide from the previous note, chosen 55% of the time on leaps of 2 or more semitones), 2 kan (a grace note from above, 40% on stressed notes). Tabla follows the tala's bol per beat ( tala.py ). Beat 1 (sam) is loudest (1.0), the khali beat is softer (0.7), others 0.82. Every fourth avartan ends with a four-stroke fill (Dha Ge Na Ti). Lyrics are spread over the gat (or over the whole song for a poem), one line per equal slot; [Mukhda] -style tags become timed headings with no duration. Tempo is clamped 40 to 180 bpm, duration 30 to 240 s. The same seed always gives the same song. After composing, if human=True , physics.humanise and autotune.score run (the tihai is exempt so sam stays exact). The result is recorded in meta.physics (engine, rubato limit, mean auto-tune correction in cents, GAN phrases used and their mean score). Fixed on 15 Nov 2026. In short talas (keherwa, dadra, adi, rupak, the bhajan talas) the whole pakad used to fill every cycle, so the gat repeated one motif and the GAN was never reached. The backend, file by file Folder: tool_layer_mhraga/mhraaga-cloud/api/ . One Lambda (Python 3.12, x86_64) behind API Gateway. Standard library plus boto3 only; the Box2D wheel is added at deploy time. local_server.py runs the same handler on your laptop with a JSON-file database ( python3 api/local_server.py , http://localhost:8787). handler.py — the front door handler(event) routes by method and path under /api , turns ApiError into {"error": ...} , and never leaks internals (an unexpected error is logged and returns a plain 500). Concern How Access If ORIGIN_SECRET is set, the x-origin-verify header must match it (CloudFront adds it), so the raw API Gateway address answers 403. Accounts signup and login . Passwords are hashed with scrypt (n=2^14, r=8, p=1, random 16-byte salt). A token is a 7-day HS256-signed JWT with the email as subject. Eight wrong passwords lock an account for 10 minutes. A disabled account cannot sign in and its tokens stop working. Quota take_quota allows 30 songs per user per day ( DAILY_COMPOSE_LIMIT ), or the user's own limit if an administrator set one. Compose make_song : checks the text against the rules ( studio.check ), takes quota, builds the brief, gets the raga, composes the score, saves it, returns it. Songs list_songs , get_song , delete_song (your own); the shared playlist is the owner playlist#common and is readable without sign-in. Plays and downloads are counted with an atomic ADD . Other routes /translate , /rules , /people , /story/* , /films , /film/plan , /tts , /teams , /admin . Secrets Read from SSM Parameter Store on first use and cached for the life of the container. studio.py — rules, people, stories, films Rules : DEFAULT_RULES (principles, blocked terms, blocked impersonation phrases, maximum prompt length) are kept as rules/ethics.json in S3 with a version history. check(*texts) runs on every prompt, lyric, story topic, translation and profile text and returns 422 on a violation. Administrators edit them with PUT /rules . learned_defaults(language) returns the tala, lead and tempo the offline factory found work best. People : voice profiles with consent. A profile stores a name, a consent note, up to 20 audio samples (S3 samples/ , each at most 2.5 MB) and style notes learned from a pasted transcript ( people_learn ); nothing is downloaded from anywhere. Profiles are for you or people who agreed, and are never used to clone a voice. Stories and pravachan : story_outline then story_section write a long spoken piece (1 to 30 minutes) section by section, limited to 80 model calls per user per day. Films : film_plan expands a short idea into a director's brief and a storyboard of scenes with effects (glow, vignette, grain, blur, light leak, particles, slow zoom, fade, black and white, warm, cool) using two model calls. film_save/get/delete keep projects up to 330 KB. team.py — shared studio Up to 150 members and 300 layers per project, all stored in the songs table: Key (owner / id) Meaning team#

mhRaaga API (for developers) Base URL: https://www.mhraaga.in/api (the same API the website and the Android app use). JSON in, JSON out. Read this first There are no API keys. Access is by user account. Create an account, sign in, and send the token. Each account has its own quota (30 songs per day), so one developer cannot spend another's. Call it from a server, a script or the app, not from another website's JavaScript. The API sends no CORS headers ( connect-src 'self' ), so a browser page on another domain is blocked. A backend or mobile client works. Be gentle. The API is throttled (about 20 requests per second overall, 2 per second on sign-in). Eight wrong passwords lock an account for 10 minutes. Use one account per integration and keep the token (it is valid 7 days). Songs are created by a hosted language model plus a rule-based composer. It costs money per song, which is why there is a daily cap. Quick start B = https://www.mhraaga.in/api # 1. create an account (once), or log in TOKEN = $( curl -s $B /auth/signup -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name":"My App","email":"me@example.com","password":"a-long-password"}' | python3 -c 'import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["token"])' ) # TOKEN=$(curl -s $B/auth/login -d '{"email":"me@example.com","password":"a-long-password"}' ...) # 2. compose a song curl -s $B /compose -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"prompt":"a calm morning bhajan to Krishna","language":"hindi","duration":120}' > song.json # 3. the score is in song.json (notes, tabla, lyrics); render it with web/synth.js (Web Audio) or lib/synth.dart (Dart) Endpoints Auth = send Authorization: Bearer <token> . t: Sound: why it is meant to sound natural
x: Sound: why it is meant to sound natural The first synth used bare oscillators: a sine flute, a sawtooth harmonium, a plain tone for the strings. That is why songs sounded electronic. Each instrument is now a small physical model (web web/synth.js , Android lib/synth.dart , same design). Instrument Model Tanpura, veena Karplus-Strong plucked string: a delay loop with loss, so the attack and the fade of the highs are real; a soft clip stands in for the jawari bridge, bright at first and mellowing as the string quietens. A veena meend is a real slide of the sounding string. Bansuri A blown tube: strong fundamental, weak overtones, a chiff of air at the start, breath noise through the note, vibrato that begins after the note, slow pitch drift, an unslurred note scooped up into pitch. Harmonium Reed spectrum, two reed banks slightly out of tune plus an octave bank, uneven bellows pressure, wooden body resonances at 700 and 2100 Hz. Tabla Dayan: Sa with harmonic partials that decay at different rates, skin slap and rim click. Bayan: a boom whose pitch rises, a wet thud, a muted ka. No two strokes the same. Manjira Brass cymbals (inharmonic partials), soft, on the beat in devotional songs (web). Room A stereo impulse response with pre-delay and early reflections, and a tail that darkens as it fades. Master Soft tape-style saturation, a gentle top-end roll-off, a low shelf, compressor and limiter. Playing Timing jitter of a few milliseconds, velocity variation, and a dynamic arc: a quiet alap that grows, a gat that swells and settles with each phrase, a strong tihai. Measured (45 s of the same bhajan score, old synth against new, against 5 reference tracks in ~/library ) old new reference tracks 95% of energy below 345 Hz 620 Hz 410 to 880 Hz Spectral flatness (richness) 0.004 0.025 0.007 to 0.049 Loudness range, 1 s windows 3.9 dB 8 dB 5 to 16 dB These are numbers about timbre and dynamics. The reference recordings were only measured, never copied or sampled. Mix balance (measured, 80 s of the bhajan, alap and gat) Rendering each part alone showed the tanpura 20 dB under the flute, so the drone was almost inaudible. I raised it 10 dB. Now: the tanpura is about 11 dB under the flute, the tabla about 3 dB under it, and the overall level is unchanged. The flute leads, the drone gives the floor, the tabla keeps time. Limits These are models, not recordings. They sound far less electronic than before, but a recording of a real player is still better. The way to go further is a library of properly licensed instrument samples, or a hosted music model (a GPU service). Neither is included. The voice speaks the words; it does not sing them to the melody.

AI voice Songs, poems, bhajans, stories, pravachan, the Speech tab and film narration use a neural voice: real audio the browser mixes with the music, instead of the device's own speech. The device voice is still there as a fallback and as a choice ("Device voice"). How it works The browser asks POST /api/tts {text, lang, style, voice} for each line (at most 320 characters). The Lambda ( api/voice.py ) looks for the audio in S3 ( tts/<hash>.wav ). A hit is free and shared by every user. A miss calls an OpenRouter audio model with a strict "read this text word for word, add nothing" prompt, wraps the PCM as a 24 kHz WAV, stores it, and returns its URL. The browser ( neural.js ) downloads and decodes the WAV and schedules it with WebAudio: reverb shared with the raga, the music ducked 8 dB under each line, a limiter on the output, no two lines overlapping (a late line is nudged after the previous one; a long line is sped up at most 20%). If anything fails (no key, daily cap, offline, a line that will not generate) that line is spoken by the device voice, so nothing goes silent. Downloaded MP3 and WAV files now include the AI voice, and so does the film WebM export. The Android player does the same natively ( lib/player.dart ): it fetches the lines, plays them on a second player, and ducks the music. Models and cost Devotional and poem text ( bhajan , song , poem , pravachan ) uses openai/gpt-audio , about $0.005 per spoken line. Stories, explainers, the Speech tab and film narration use openai/gpt-audio-mini , about $0.0003 per line. If the mini model returns audio far longer than the text should take (it once added extra sentences), the line is redone on the full model. The whole build and test of this feature, with retries, cost about $0.51. Caps (environment variables, defaults): TTS_USER_DAILY_USD=0.60 per user per day, TTS_SITE_DAILY_USD=12 for the whole site per day. Only new generations count; cached lines are free. Change models with TTS_MODEL and TTS_MODEL_MINI . Voices: male = onyx, female = shimmer. Measured quality (not listening) Each language was spoken, then transcribed back by a separate model call and compared with the original text: Hindi 96%, Marathi 95%, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Kannada and English 100%. The differences are mostly spelling variants, but a human who knows the language should still listen. Mix of the two sample songs, rendered offline: voice 3 to 6 dB above the ducked music, peak 0.94, no clipped samples, no overlapping lines. Limits It speaks, it does not sing to the melody. The melody is the raga lead under it. It needs the OpenRouter key and costs money per new line. When a daily cap is reached the device voice takes over. The upstream service rate-limits bursts; the server retries with backoff and the browser asks for two lines at a time, so a brand-new song takes about 15 to 40 seconds to prepare the first time. t: Physics, auto-tune, GAN phrases and the shared studio
x: Physics, auto-tune, GAN phrases and the shared studio Song engine (music_engine_framework_layer/mhraaga_engine) compose() builds the raga score from grammar (alap, gat, tihai), then three stages shape it: GAN phrases ( gan.py ). A small generative adversarial network (generator 6-16-8, discriminator 8-16-1) trained on about 1,800 eight-note phrases harvested from the grammar of every classical raga, a sample of melakartas and gopi ragas ( agentic/train_gan.py , numpy, offline). Weights ship in gan_weights.json ; inference is plain Python so the Lambda needs no numpy. About 30% of gat phrases come from the generator, snapped to the raga's own notes so they cannot leave the raga. Honest limit: it learns the grammar's phrase shapes, not taste. After training the discriminator scores real and generated phrases about equally (0.5), so its score is a weak filter, not a quality judge. Physics ( physics.py ). Runs on the real Box2D engine (pybox2d 2.3.10, the C++ library) wherever it can be imported, which is the deployed Lambda (python3.12, x86_64; the wheel is fetched by deploy.sh ). It drives: rubato (a body on a Box2D wheel-joint spring, kicked by phrase endings and sampled at the next note; at most 28 ms, about 10 ms in practice), weight (a ball dropped under gravity onto an edge fixture with restitution; the speed at impact sets the dynamic, so leaps strike harder, and stressed vadi/samvadi notes are heavier), meend glide time (a critically damped spring whose mass grows with the interval, 0.15 to 0.25 s) and a slow pitch wander . If Box2D cannot be imported (a laptop without the wheel) the same models run on a small pure-Python solver using the same algorithms; the two agree to about 1 ms. Every score records which one ran in meta.physics.engine . The tihai is never moved, so the last note lands exactly on sam. Auto-tune ( autotune.py ). Pulls every lead note toward the nearest in-raga shruti (just intonation) by 75%, and hard-snaps the tihai. It also offers track() for a recorded pitch track with a dead-band that keeps vibrato. Notes are now [time, hz, duration, ornament, velocity, glide] . Old four-field scores still play. compose(..., human=False) turns physics off. The score's meta.physics reports what was applied. The web synth, the offline MP3 export and the Android synth all read velocity. Shared studio (api/team.py, web/team.html, web/team.js) One film or song project, up to 150 people and 300 layers. A layer is one film shot or one song section, owned by one artist. Role Can director everything: add or remove people, reorder, approve, render, delete the project artist create (up to 8) and edit only their own layers, set them to review, comment viewer read and comment Conflicts: every layer save carries the revision it was based on. If someone changed the layer first the save fails with 409 and the editor reloads their version. Nobody overwrites anyone silently. t: Studio features and what was not integrated
x: Studio features and what was not integrated Built into the site and API: spoken poems, stories / pravachan / explainers (1 to 30 minutes, written section by section by the model, narrated by the device's voices over a raga bed), People (consent, voice samples, speaking-style notes learned from pasted transcripts), AI rules in S3 ( rules/ethics.json , editable by an administrator, versioned in rules/history/ ), and the self-learning loop ( rules/learned.json feeds default tāla, tempo and instrument per language). The Android app has songs, poems and speech; stories, People and Studio are web-only for now. Not copied into this project, on purpose: - VoiceStudio (debpalash/voicestudio) is AGPL-3.0 and needs local GPU models. Embedding it in a hosted service would put this whole service under AGPL. Run it separately on your own machine with the exported samples. - Explainroo, VUZA and agnes-video-generator (MIT) are local Python/Node pipelines that render video with local models and ffmpeg. They do not run in Lambda. The site's Explainer produces the script and on-screen points and plays them; making an exported MP4 needs one of these on a machine with ffmpeg and a speech model. VUZA's Pinterest scraping is a terms-of-service risk and was not used. - YouTube links : the site does not download or transcribe videos. Paste a transcript (Show transcript) into a person's profile and it learns the style from that text. Links you add are kept as notes only. - Voice cloning and cloned-voice songs or videos : the browser and phone cannot do it, and nothing here clones a voice. Putting mhraaga.in on the site The site is served by CloudFront ( https://d1bka1wc4jd8uy.cloudfront.net ). A custom domain needs a certificate and two DNS records. The template already has the switches ( DomainName , CertificateArn ). Certificate (must be in us-east-1, even though the stack is in ap-south-1). bash aws acm request-certificate --region us-east-1 --domain-name mhraaga.in --subject-alternative-names www.mhraaga.in --validation-method DNS --profile default aws acm describe-certificate --region us-east-1 --certificate-arn <ARN> --query 'Certificate.DomainValidationOptions[].ResourceRecord' Validate: add the CNAME records it prints at your domain registrar's DNS. Wait until the status is ISSUED (a few minutes). Deploy with the domain: bash DOMAIN_NAME=mhraaga.in CERT_ARN=<ARN> AWS_PROFILE=default bash tool_layer_mhraga/mhraaga-cloud/infra/deploy.sh (or put DOMAIN_NAME= and CERT_ARN= in .env ). The output CloudFrontDomain is your CloudFront address. Point DNS at CloudFront: www → CNAME to the CloudFront address. The bare mhraaga.in needs an ALIAS/ANAME record (Route 53 offers this as an A/AAAA alias; many registrars do not). If your registrar has no ALIAS, move the domain's DNS to Route 53 (create a hosted zone, change the nameservers at the registrar, add the alias records). Test https://mhraaga.in . HSTS is on, so keep HTTPS working before announcing it. Leaving the two variables empty keeps the CloudFront address, so nothing breaks until you are ready. Every redeploy must pass them, or the aliases are removed. The singer layer (YuE2) mhRaaga's own voice speaks the words. A real sung vocal needs a singing model. The open YuE2 model (vendored in third_party/YuE ) can sing lyrics in a style over a band. The singer layer connects it to mhRaaga so the model sings our raga melody instead of inventing a tune. Status, plainly: the layer is built and tested, and its output passes YuE2's own score check. No song has been sung yet , because the model needs a GPU and this project has none. Nothing paid has been started. How the agents learn Source: music_engine_framework_layer/mhraaga_engine/agentic/evolve.py and critics.py . State is kept in agentic/data/policy.json . One round, step by step Choose. For a language, each producer draws one random number from the Beta belief of every option it has and picks the option with the highest draw. Good options win more often; options with little evidence still get a chance, because their belief is wide. Compose. The composer turns the seven genes into a song. Judge. The eight critics score it. The song's reward is the weighted sum (weights in the agents page ). Quality per agent. Each producer's quality is the mean of the scores of the critics that judge its work (for example tempo is judged by rhythm and library_affinity ). Share the credit. Kalkee's Shapley function splits the song's reward among the producers (below). Update. For the option a producer picked, its belief moves: alpha += p and beta += 1 - p , where p is its credit scaled so that an equal share equals the song's own reward and clamped to 0 to 1. Next time that option is a little more or less likely to be drawn. Thompson sampling in one picture Every option holds a Beta(alpha, beta) belief that starts at Beta(1, 1), "no idea". Each success adds to alpha, each failure to beta. The mean is alpha / (alpha + beta). Drawing from the belief, not using the mean, is what keeps the agents exploring. The Shapley credit split A song is the work of seven agents together. Giving the whole reward to the last agent, or splitting it evenly, would teach them the wrong thing. The Shapley value gives each agent the average of what it adds across every order in which the agents could have joined. - The value of a group is modelled as a noisy-OR of its members' qualities: v(S) = 1 - product(1 - quality_i) . Two decent agents together are worth more than either alone, but not the sum. - With up to 8 agents the value is computed exactly (there are 7 here); above that a Monte Carlo estimate is used. - The reward is split in proportion to each agent's share, so the credits add up to the reward exactly. - If every quality is about zero, the reward is split evenly so nothing divides by zero. The catalogue At most 100 songs , about 14 per language (Hindi, Marathi, English, Telugu, Gujarati, Kannada, Tamil). A new song enters if its language has room, or if its reward beats the weakest song of that language by more than 0.003 (then it replaces it). Improvement: the weakest songs of each language are re-made with new seeds and one gene re-drawn from the beliefs; a variant replaces its parent only if it scores higher. At least three spoken poems per language are kept. What this does and does not do It lifted the mean critic reward from 0.862 to 0.969 in the first runs. That is a number about the critics' rules. It is not a measure of how good a song sounds to a person. Listen, and use the Create page's Styles box to steer what the live site makes.

How the system works mhRaaga turns a sentence into a raga song, with the words spoken over it. This page walks through it from the click to the sound, then shows the machinery behind it. The story of one song 1 You describe it a sentence, or your lyrics 2 Brief language model plans it 3 Raga + tala from 16,000 ragas 4 Score alap, gat, tihai 5 Feel Box2D, GAN, auto-tune 6 Instruments played on your device 7 Voice neural speech, cached 8 Mix ducking, limiter You describe it. "A calm morning bhajan to Krishna", or paste your own lyrics. You can pick a language, a lead instrument, a tala and a length. The brief. A hosted language model (via OpenRouter) turns that into a plan: raga, tala, tempo, mood, language and lyrics. If the model is down, keyword rules still make a plan, so a song is always produced. The raga and the tala. The engine knows 30 classical ragas, all 72 melakartas and the 16,000 "gopi" ragas (a pair of melakartas, one of three tonics, a janya cut). Each has an ascent, a descent, a vadi and samvadi, and a time of day. The score. The composer writes the classical form: alap (the drone and free flute), gat (the tabla enters; each cycle opens on sam ; the vadi is held; meend and kan ornaments), then a tihai that lands exactly on sam . Lyrics are timed to the phrases. The feel. Real physics makes it human: a Box2D spring gives rubato, a falling ball gives each note its weight, another spring gives the meend glide. A small GAN offers fresh phrases. Auto-tune pulls every note toward its shruti, and the last note is snapped exactly to Sa. The instruments. The score is plain JSON. Your device plays it with physical models: plucked-string tanpura, breathy bansuri, reed harmonium, tabla from its modes, a room reverb, human timing and dynamics. The voice. Each lyric line is spoken by a neural voice model. The audio is made once, stored in S3 and shared by everyone, so the second listener pays nothing and waits nothing. If the voice service is busy, your device's own voice reads that line instead. The mix. The browser lays the voice over the music, turns the music down under each line, and runs a limiter so nothing clips. Downloads (MP3 or WAV) include the voice.
